title: Twice as far from the lamp
hook: Move your book twice as far from a lamp. Does it get half as bright?

knows: lamps look dimmer from farther away
area of a square is side times side
doesNotKnow: that light spreads over an area
the lux as a unit of illuminance

misconception: Double the distance, half the brightness.
objective: The learner can explain that light from a small source spreads over an area that grows with the square of distance, so at twice the distance a surface gets a quarter of the light.

claims.text: Light from a small source spreads over an area that grows with the square of the distance, so brightness on a page facing it falls as 1 / distance^2.
claims.source: Inverse-square law for a point source: illuminance E = I / d^2 (for a surface facing the source), because the same flux crosses a sphere of area 4 pi d^2. Hecht, Optics, ch. 3; Halliday, Resnick and Walker, ch. 33 (intensity of a point source).

claims.text: 100 lux at 1 m becomes 25 lux at 2 m and about 11 lux at 3 m (44.4 lux at 1.5 m, 16 lux at 2.5 m).
A beam that is 1 m wide at 1 m is 2 m wide and 2 m tall at 2 m, so it covers 4 page-sized squares; at 3 m, 9.
claims.source: Similar triangles: straight rays from a point, so width is proportional to distance and area to distance squared.

claims.text: The lux is a unit of illuminance: one lumen of light falling on each square metre.
claims.source: SI derived unit lux = lm/m^2 (BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed., Table 4).

claims.text: The law holds for a small lamp with no walls bouncing light back; a large lamp, or a room's walls, make light fall off more slowly up close.
claims.source: Stated idealisation: point source in empty space. The inverse-square law is accurate for distances greater than about five times the source size (a common photometry rule of thumb: treat a source as a point beyond about five times its size).

recall.question: A plant 1 m from a grow lamp gets plenty of light. You move it to 3 m. Roughly what share of the light does it get now?
recall.why: Light spreads over an area that grows with distance squared: three times the distance, nine times the area, a ninth of the light.
